sentences.text: The Rodrigues parrot, scientifically named Necropsittacus rodricanus, was an extinct parrot species that lived exclusively on the island of Rodrigues. It stood out as the largest parrot species on the island, distinguished by a notably large head and a long tail. Its feathers displayed a uniform green coloration throughout its body.
To escape introduced rats, this bird frequented and nested on offshore islets where these predators were absent.
By 1671, the bird had already become rare and was considered popular game by hunters.
The bird was first mentioned by French traveler François Leguat in his 1708 memoir, A New Voyage to the East Indies.

In 1867, French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bones of the Rodrigues parrot received via British ornithologist Alfred Newton. He scientifically named the species Psittacus rodricanus based on a fragmentary upper beak.
After receiving more complete beak remains in 1873, Milne-Edwards moved the species to the genus Necropsittacus, which he had established in 1874.
Subfossil remains of the Rodrigues parrot have been found in caves on the Plaine Corail and in Caverne Tortue.
British ecologists Anthony S. Cheke and Hume proposed that Mascarene parrots, like the dodo, may have derived from South Asian ancestors.
The Rodrigues parrot is classified as a member of the tribe Psittaculini, though its closest relative among other species is unclear.
The genus Necropsittacus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The species is known only from subfossil remains and mentions in contemporary accounts.

The Rodrigues parrot was last mentioned in 1761 and likely went extinct soon after due to introduced predators, deforestation, and human hunting. The last known mention of the species was in 1761, and it likely became extinct shortly thereafter.

Julian Hume suggested in 2007 that Leguat's mention of green and blue parrots could refer to both the Rodrigues parrot and Newton's parakeet, or represent color morphs of the parakeet. Samuel Pasfield Oliver doubted in 1891 that the parrots mentioned by Leguat were the Rodrigues parrot, suggesting they were actually Newton's parakeet due to size differences.

In 1893, E. Newton and Hans Gadow found the Rodrigues parrot closely related to the broad-billed parrot but could not determine if they belonged in the same genus due to missing crest evidence. Graham S. Cowles found the skulls of the Rodrigues parrot and broad-billed parrot too dissimilar to be close relatives in 1987.

In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested that the species N. borbonicus might have been an escaped pet lory rather than a wild bird. In 2007, Hume suggested that Rothschild mistakenly linked N. borbonicus to the Rodrigues parrot by incorporating Dubois's account into the latter's description.
